# Score-Based Diffusion: A One-Dimensional Learning Sequence {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## Retired material

This earlier tutorial sequence is retained for reference. The current teaching
sequence is [Probability-Flow ODE, Parts 1–5](./07-probability-flow-ode.qmd)
(Lectures 12–16). Follow those lectures for the current notation, derivations,
and notebook exercises. These older notes contain additional background but
are no longer part of the main reading sequence.
:::

Begin with particles on a line. Derive how their motion transports probability,
then add random motion and study its effect on the density. Only after solving
these problems do we learn an unknown score or introduce higher dimensions.

The entry prerequisites are derivatives, integrals, Taylor expansion, elementary
probability, and Gaussian distributions. No prior SDE, stochastic-calculus, PDE,
or fluid-mechanics course is assumed. The ODE and SDE tutorials are stand-alone;
the SDE tutorial includes the deterministic recap it needs.

## Archived reading order

| Part | Tutorial | Central question |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [ODEs in One Dimension: Particles, Flows, and Densities](./25-learning-the-score.qmd) | How does a local velocity move each particle and its population density? |
| 2 | [SDEs in One Dimension: Brownian Motion, Itô Calculus, and Langevin Sampling](./26-probability-flow-sampling.qmd) | How do random kicks change conservation, and why does balanced noise make score-based sampling possible? |
| 3 | [Score-Based Diffusion in One Dimension: Corruption, Sampling, and Denoising](./27-diffusion-neural-odes-normalizing-flows.qmd) | How can the score reverse a prescribed density path, and how can we learn it? |
| 4 | [From One-Dimensional Transport to Neural ODEs and Higher Dimensions](./28-langevin-dynamics.qmd) | How do these transports connect to normalizing flows, and what changes in several dimensions? |

Each worked model links **particle dynamics, its solution, the density, and a
conservation/Fokker–Planck check**. The examples repeat deliberately: standard
normal, shifted normal, arbitrary Gaussian variance, and a smooth two-Gaussian
mixture. Long calculations are derivation subsections; optional connections
are identified as such. Exact Gaussian solutions precede numerical mixtures.

The figures show arrows, paths, and population densities. The reproducible
[simulation script](../materials/one-dimensional-score-examples.py) generates
the four figures and checks the Gaussian formulas. Existing interactive practice
is available in the [score-flow lab](../materials/score-flow-lab.html).

## Shared symbols

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_t$, $X_t$ | One trajectory, and a random state respectively |
| $q_t(x)$ | Current population or generic sampler density |
| $p(x)$ | One fixed target density |
| $p_t(x)$ | Prescribed forward-corruption density in Tutorial 3 |
| $s(x)=\partial_x\log p(x)$, $s_t(x)=\partial_x\log p_t(x)$ | Fixed-target and time-dependent scores |
| $v(x,t)$ | ODE velocity |
| $f(x,t)$, $g(t)$ | SDE drift and spatially constant noise amplitude |
| $W_t$ | Standard Brownian motion |
| $\Psi_{r\to t}$ | Flow map from time $r$ to time $t$ |
| $J(x,t)$ | Signed probability flux |
| $m_t$, $V_t$, $a_t=\sqrt{V_t}$ | Gaussian population mean, variance, standard deviation |
| $\mu$, $a^2$ | Fixed Gaussian target mean and variance |
| $\alpha_t$, $\sigma_t^2$ | Corruption signal coefficient and conditional noise variance |
| $\epsilon$, $\xi_k$ | Noise in one corruption observation; fresh numerical-step noises |
| $\Phi$ | Standard normal CDF; never a flow map |
| $F_t$ | CDF of $p_t$; never a flow map |
| $\beta(t)$ | VP corruption schedule |
| $\tau=T-t$ | Increasing generation clock |
| $u$, $B_u$ | Fixed-level Langevin clock and its Brownian motion |
| $s_\theta(x,t)$ | Learned marginal-score approximation |
| $\pi_T$ | Chosen terminal law, potentially approximating $p_T$ |
| $\lambda(t)$ | Positive weight on a time-indexed training loss |
| $\widehat X_k$ | Numerical approximation to an SDE state |
| $\widehat x_0(x,t)$ | Posterior-mean clean-data denoiser |
| $DF$ | Jacobian matrix of a map, introduced only in the final extension |

The first three tutorials use scalar states and $\partial_x$, never vector
notation. Tutorial 4 explicitly introduces $d$-dimensional vectors, gradient,
divergence, and Laplacian after completing its one-dimensional discussion.

## Time and sign conventions

In Tutorial 1, $t$ is ordinary ODE evolution time. In Tutorial 2 it is SDE or
Langevin algorithmic time; the Langevin target $p$ stays fixed. In Tutorial 3,
$t$ labels **forward corruption from data to noise**, and $\tau=T-t$ is an
increasing clock for generation. A separate $u$ is used only when running a
fixed-target Langevin corrector while holding the corruption level $t$ fixed.

The straight-path flow-matching example in Tutorial 4 explicitly uses source-to-data
time and then switches back to the corruption convention for Gaussian paths.

Every numerical step magnitude $h$ is positive. Backward ODE integration uses
$-h v$; reverse-SDE noise has scale $g\sqrt h$. The
[Song convention comparison](./27-diffusion-neural-odes-normalizing-flows.qmd#song-sde-conventions)
explains how this relates to a reverse SDE written with negative $dt$.

## Three distinctions to carry through the series

1. Increasing density at an individual particle's location is not the same as
   producing the correct population distribution. A bare Gaussian score ODE
   contracts; an appropriately designed ODE can transport the entire distribution.
2. A fixed density being stationary under an SDE does not by itself prove
   convergence from another initial distribution or accuracy of a finite-step sampler.
3. Equal one-time marginal densities do not mean equal paths or equal endpoint
   couplings. This is the link between stochastic diffusion and deterministic flow.

[From Local Arrows](./22-vector-fields-to-score-diffusion.qmd) and
